analysis.title: Markets Observer Q4 2026 (Manager Research, data as of Sept. 30, 2026)
key_insights: Bonds fell across the board in Q3 2026 as inflation, deficit concerns and the September Fed rate hike pushed yields up and prices down. Equities sputtered in Q3 but remain broadly positive for the year.
US small-cap stocks fell 5.6% in Q3 as investors favored larger companies in a rising rate environment. The US market gained about 1% in Q3 and roughly 12% year to date.
Bitcoin rose 42.6% in Q3, reversing a decline that began in October 2025. Oil rose 41.9% over the quarter, and commodities gained 39.7% from June's trough.

The US stock expansion is now 33 months old. Since the 2022 downturn the US market has gained 30.7% annualized and 108.8% in total. A few market leaders, mostly AI stocks, have lifted benchmarks while many smaller stocks lagged.
Trailing 12-month returns: commodities 39.7%, emerging-market stocks 25.2%, developed ex-US stocks 15.4%, US stocks 14.9%, emerging-market bonds -0.9%, US bonds -2.1%.
Energy stocks rose 15% in Q3 and nearly 40% year to date as the Iran war passed the seven-month mark. Utilities and industrials each fell about 12% in Q3 on higher rates.
Developed international stocks gained 1.3% in Q3 and emerging markets fell 0.9%, versus 9.5% and 22.4% in Q2. Developed Asia ex-Japan and Japan led, while inflation weighed on Europe ex-UK.

Valuation-implied 10-year returns: emerging-market stocks have the second-highest expected return. US high yield has the highest, with its estimate up 1.4 percentage points despite a weak quarter for fixed income.
South Korea is up 74.5% year to date on semiconductor and memory-chip stocks. Thailand, Peru, Greece and Egypt each gained more than 25%. China, India and South Africa are negative year to date.

In 2026 year-to-date return decomposition, Asia ex-Japan and emerging markets led on improved margins despite lower P/E multiples. Europe ex-UK trailed on currency pressure and weaker margin expansion.
Energy and technology led sectors on sales growth and margin expansion. Consumer discretionary was hit hardest as falling valuation multiples outweighed better profitability.

The median US stock ended September at an 8.1% discount to Morningstar fair value. Communication services was the most undervalued sector, followed by consumer cyclicals and real estate. Healthcare was the most overvalued.

The large-cap over small-cap P/E premium briefly fell below its average in July for the first time since May 2021 and rose again in September. Semiconductors' valuation lead over software reversed sharply from June on concerns about AI spending and earnings.
Value and momentum were the top factors over the past year, though momentum weakened in Q3. Quality, low volatility and size posted modestly negative returns.
Korea and Taiwan semiconductor stocks drove most of the Morningstar Emerging Markets Index's 12-month rise, while India and China detracted.
Midterm election years have on average been followed by stronger 12-month stock returns than presidential or nonelection years over 50 years.

Fixed-income sectors fell in Q3 except leveraged loans. Munis were also hurt by heavy new-issue supply. Most sectors are negative over 12 months, with credit-heavy and less rate-sensitive sectors the exception.
The Treasury curve bear steepened in Q3 on oil-driven inflation fears, debt-funded AI data center spending, and the Fed's 25-basis-point hike in September.
The 10-year Treasury yield ended Q3 at 5.29%, a multidecade high. The ECB, BOJ and RBA each raised rates by 25 basis points during the quarter, and the Bank of England held.

The 10-year real yield rose sharply in 2026 to 2.93% while the 10-year breakeven rose only slightly to 2.36%. Morningstar reads this as growth and competition for capital, not inflation fear or loss of faith in US debt.

Spreads on CCC rated bank loans widened to 2,183.76 basis points, levels last seen shortly after the 2020 selloff, while BB and B spreads were flat or tighter. Many CCC loans were originated in 2021-22 and are nearing maturity with higher default risk.
Mortgage rates passed 7.25%, the highest since 2023, rising 25 basis points in the last week of September, the largest weekly rise since 2022. MBS lost value and agency mortgage spreads widened.
September was the worst month for municipal bonds since 2008, and the Morningstar US Municipal Bond Index fell 6% in the quarter on macro pressure and weak technicals, not credit deterioration.

Digital asset funds rose 43.9% in Q3 but are still down 26.9% over 12 months. Utilities fell 12.1% in Q3. Taxable-bond funds took the largest inflows while US equity and allocation funds saw outflows.
Leveraged single-stock and sector ETFs had 218 new launches in the first half of 2026, far above any other category.
Commodity fund inflows reached USD 11 billion in August 2026 after five months of outflows. Inflation-protected bond funds took in USD 6 billion in August.
Thematic ETFs have taken in about USD 76 billion since December 2024, with AI and Big Data drawing about USD 26 billion.

Morningstar expects US GDP growth to slow through 2028 on decelerating AI spending, slower population growth and high rates, then rebound in 2029-30. Inflation should recede as oil and tariff shocks fade.

Morningstar expects another Fed hike before year-end, rate cuts from the second half of 2027, and a fed-funds rate of 2.50%-2.75% by end-2028 versus 3.75%-4.00% now. It sees the 10-year yield at 3.25% by 2029.
Futures-implied policy rates rose versus June 30 for the Fed, ECB and BOJ as central banks focus on above-target inflation despite solid growth.
The IMF projects global GDP growth of 3.1% in 2026 (3.5% in 2025), 3.4% in 2027, then 3.1% by 2031. The 2026 slowdown is mostly Middle Eastern oil producers hit by the Iran war.
Gasoline and diesel prices have doubled or more versus prewar levels, with wide crack spreads. Futures imply a large price fall over the next year, which would limit a lasting inflationary effect.

Morningstar argues bond market inflation expectations have barely risen even as gold rallied, so currency debasement fears are unlikely to be driving yields. It attributes the 2026 yield rise mainly to AI-driven economic strength.

Morningstar's regression suggests that at Denmark's 27% debt/GDP the 2026 rise in 10-year Treasury yields would be 0.7 points instead of 1.1, so debt concerns matter but explain a minority of the rise. French-German 10-year spreads jumped about 0.4 points from mid-September.

AI-related investment is a growing share of US GDP growth, but Morningstar says the Fed's higher rates offset it by crowding out residential and nontech business investment, so AI's main effect is on interest rates.
US home price growth slowed to 2.1% in Q2 2026 from 2.9% in 2025 and 5.4% in 2024. Midwestern markets are more resilient and Sunbelt markets are weak or negative.

sector_views.rationale: Energy stocks rose 15% in Q3 and nearly 40% year to date as oil prices surged during the Iran war. This is a performance description, not a formal Morningstar recommendation.
Utilities fell about 12% in Q3 as higher rates weighed on rate-sensitive sectors. This describes performance, not a formal Morningstar recommendation.

macro_indicators.interpretation: The Fed hiked 25 basis points unanimously in September, resuming tightening. Morningstar expects another hike before year-end.

macro_indicators.interpretation: Cuts are expected to resume in the second half of 2027, a net 1.25 percentage points below the current range.
A multidecade high, driven by real yields, AI-related borrowing and Fed tightening.
Lower policy rates are expected to pull long-term yields down.
Real yields drove most of the 2026 rise in 10-year yields.
Market inflation expectations rose only slightly, so investors are not pricing runaway inflation.
Highest since 2023, up 25 basis points in the last week of September.
The previous reading as of 6/30/2026 was 3.90%, showing tighter expected policy.

crypto_views: Bitcoin rose 42.6% in Q3 2026, reversing a decline that began in October 2025.
Digital asset funds gained 43.9% in Q3 but are down 26.9% over 12 months.
Digital Assets is among the Morningstar fund categories with a large number of ETF launches in 2026.
risk_factors: Persistent inflation and a possible further Fed hike keep pressure on bonds and rate-sensitive sectors.
Market concentration in a few AI stocks, and in Korea and Taiwan semiconductor stocks within emerging markets, leaves benchmarks exposed to those names.
CCC rated loans face default risk as 2021-22 vintages approach maturity at higher rates.
Government debt worries are increasing, shown by the jump in the French-German spread.
Concerns about AI spending and earnings triggered a semiconductor selloff and valuation reset from June.
Mortgage rates above 7.25% strain housing, and Sunbelt home prices are weak or negative.
The Iran war and refinery disruptions could keep energy prices elevated.
charts_described: Chart on the yield curve shows the Treasury curve higher on Sept. 30, 2026 than on June 30, 2026 and Sept. 30, 2025.
Chart on 10-year real yield and breakeven shows real yield at 2.93% and breakeven at 2.36%.
Chart on leveraged loan spreads shows CCC at 2,183.76 basis points, B at 412.49 and BB at 256.15.
Chart on global 10-year yields shows UK 5.41%, Australia 5.34%, US 5.29%, Germany 3.57% and Japan 3.08%.
Chart on emerging-market attribution shows Korea at 130.4% and Taiwan at 85.5% cumulative return versus 26.2% for the Morningstar Emerging Markets Index.
Chart on trailing 12-month asset class performance shows commodities 39.7%, emerging-market stocks 25.2%, developed ex-US 15.4%, US stocks 14.9%, emerging-market bonds -0.9% and US bonds -2.1%.
vol_and_positioning: Momentum weakened notably in Q3 as the best performers early in the year pulled back.
Rate volatility hurt mortgage-backed securities because of their negative convexity.
Leveraged single-stock and sector ETFs, meant for holding hours or days, saw 218 launches in the first half of 2026.
Commodity funds took USD 11 billion of inflows in August, and thematic ETFs have taken about USD 76 billion since December 2024.
The probability of an October Fed hike fell in the last two weeks of September, per CME FedWatch.
geopolitical: The Iran war has passed the seven-month mark and is pushing up oil, gasoline and diesel prices.
Refinery disruptions in Russia and elsewhere widened crack spreads.
Middle Eastern oil output has been curtailed by the Iran war, which accounts for most of the IMF's 2026 global growth downgrade.
Energy price shock and tariff effects feed inflation, with futures implying prices fall as disruptions fade.

tension_points.bull_case: Morningstar attributes the 2026 yield rise mainly to AI-driven economic strength and real yields, not fears of lost faith in US debt, with breakevens up only slightly.
tension_points.bear_case: Government debt concerns are playing a bigger role: the regression implies a 1.1 point rise versus 0.7 at Denmark's debt level, and the French-German spread widened about 0.4 points in mid-September.
tension_points.what_invalidates: A sharp rise in breakeven inflation or a further widening of high-debt countries' spreads would point to debt and inflation fears as the main driver.

tension_points.bull_case: Futures imply a hefty fall in oil and product prices over the next year, so the energy shock should not have a sustained inflationary impact.
tension_points.bear_case: Gasoline and diesel have doubled or more versus prewar levels, central banks are hiking, and above-target inflation has lasted over five years.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Oil and product futures failing to fall as disruptions persist would undercut the fading-shock view.

theme_stances.key_argument: AI-driven economic strength is the main factor behind higher US yields in 2026, with debt concerns a smaller contributor.
theme_stances.evidence: economic strength, underpinned by AI, is the main factor driving up yields

theme_stances.key_argument: Another hike is likely before year-end, then cuts resume in the second half of 2027.
theme_stances.evidence: another hike is likely before the end of the year

theme_stances.key_argument: AI spending crowds out other spending because the Fed keeps rates elevated, so AI's main effect is on interest rates.
theme_stances.evidence: AI's main effect right now is on interest rates
